turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Contemptuously, you say? Pray, enlighten me, Mr. Darcy. Do you intend to paint Mr. Wickham as a villain worthy of your dramatic pronouncements, or are you merely attempting to deflect from your own deplorable actions?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Madam, your insistence on championing a man whose character is so demonstrably flawed, whose deceit is so readily apparent to any discerning observer, is truly perplexing. I shall not engage in a theatrical performance to satisfy your prejudices, but I will endeavour to explain the truth regarding Mr. Wickham’s… *conduct*.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: The truth, Mr. Darcy? You speak as if you possess a monopoly on veracity! I daresay you have a vested interest in discrediting Mr. Wickham, given your… history. Do proceed, then, and let us see just how much of your fabricated narrative you intend to inflict upon my ears.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Madam, to suggest I *fabricate* narratives is an insult of the highest order. My concern is not to discredit Mr. Wickham for mere personal gratification, but to expose his duplicity, a duplicity which, I regret to observe, you appear remarkably inclined to overlook.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Duplicity, you say? A convenient label, Mr. Darcy, for anything that inconveniences *you*. I find it rather remarkable that you, a gentleman so accustomed to wielding power and influence, are so readily offended by a mere reflection of your own failings.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your impertinence, Miss Bennet, grows tiresome. It is not merely a matter of offense, but a fundamental misunderstanding of propriety and judgment that fuels your accusations. I find it necessary, despite the discomfort it causes me, to clarify my position, for your understanding, and, frankly, for the sake of truth.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Oh, *truth*, is it? How very noble of you to concern yourself with such a lofty ideal, Mr. Darcy, particularly when you attempt to cloak your own manipulations within its guise. Pray, enlighten me further; I am positively *dying* to hear how you justify your interference in the lives of others.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your cynicism is… disheartening. I confess, I had hoped for a degree of civility, even from one who so readily embraces falsehoods and condemns those who strive for integrity. I believe a declaration is due, though I anticipate it will be met with further scorn.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: A declaration, Mr. Darcy? From *you*? I daresay the very air in this room has grown thick with absurdity. Do proceed, then; I am eager to observe the depths of your folly.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I find your mockery profoundly unjust. Despite the provocations, despite the persistent and, I confess, increasingly painful rebuffs, I must declare, with a sincerity I scarcely believe you will comprehend, that I am, and have been for a considerable time, deeply in love with you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Love, Mr. Darcy? You insult my intelligence with such a preposterous claim! Do you truly believe a few carefully chosen phrases can erase the memory of Wickham, of Bingley, of your own arrogant pronouncements?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your continued disbelief is… vexing. I am not entirely surprised, given your predisposition to suspect the worst in others, but to dismiss my sentiments so readily, to conflate past actions with the genuine and profound affection I harbour, is an affront. I concede I have erred, and I am prepared to address those errors, but to deny the truth of my feelings is to deny a reality that exists independently of your judgment.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: An affront, you say? It is an affront to *me*, Mr. Darcy, to have my sensibilities so grossly underestimated! You speak of errors; I should think the most egregious of them was believing anyone could persuade me of such a fanciful notion as this.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your vehemence is… regrettable. I perceive that you choose to focus solely on the perceived failings of my character, neglecting entirely the demonstrable efforts I have made to rectify them – efforts, I might add, undertaken solely for your sake. I trust you will at least grant me the courtesy of explaining these actions, rather than continuing to dismiss them with such unseemly disdain.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Rectify them? You believe a few paltry gestures absolve you of years of interference and condescension? I am weary of your justifications, Mr. Darcy; they ring hollow when coupled with the blatant disregard you’ve shown for the feelings of others.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your persistence in characterizing my actions as mere 'gestures' reveals a regrettable obstinacy. I assure you, my endeavors have been born of a sincere desire to alleviate the distress caused by my previous conduct, and to demonstrate a commitment to principles far exceeding mere social convention.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Principles exceeding social convention? How very noble of you, Mr. Darcy! I daresay it's quite convenient to claim such lofty motives when attempting to excuse behaviour that would shame a tradesman, let alone a gentleman of your standing.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your flippancy is… tiresome. While I am accustomed to encountering a certain degree of levity amongst those of lesser fortune, I find it profoundly disappointing to witness it employed in such a manner by a lady of your intelligence. I am attempting, with considerable difficulty, to convey the sincerity of my regard, and your continued barbs serve only to obstruct any possibility of understanding.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Sincerity, you say? Pray, enlighten me, Mr. Darcy. Is it sincere to manipulate a man's affections, as you attempted with Mr. Wickham, or to interfere in the happiness of my dearest sister? I find your definition of sincerity remarkably… elastic.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations regarding Mr. Wickham are, as I have previously explained, founded on a profound misunderstanding of the circumstances. To suggest I *manipulated* his affections is an affront, and to imply I deliberately sought to obstruct your sister’s happiness demonstrates a regrettable lack of discernment, which I find increasingly difficult to comprehend.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: She answered him with cold civility.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His sense of her inferiority, of its being a degradation, of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: He concluded with representing to her the strength of that attachment which in spite of all his endeavours he had found impossible to conquer; and with expressing his hope that it would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! repeated Darcy, contemptuously--yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
